title: Netrin and DCC: One Cue, Two Answers

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: The moving, sensing tip of a growing axon is the {{c1::growth cone}}.
cards.quote: the growth cone (the moving, sensing tip of a growing axon; see the lesson on the growth cone)

cards.front: In the embryonic spinal cord, the floor plate lies along the {{c1::ventral midline}}.
cards.quote: The floor plate is a strip of cells along the ventral midline, at the bottom of the slice.
cards.section: The layout

cards.front: What are the progenitor cells of the embryonic spinal cord’s ventricular zone?
cards.back: Dividing cells that make neurons and glia.
cards.quote: Its cells are progenitors, dividing cells that make neurons and glia.
cards.section: The layout

cards.front: What is the basement membrane covering the pial surface of the embryonic spinal cord?
cards.back: A thin sheet of extracellular matrix covering the cord’s outer edge.
cards.quote: The pial surface is that outer edge, covered by a basement membrane, a thin sheet of extracellular matrix.
cards.section: The layout

cards.front: In netrin guidance, what determines the cue’s location and what determines attraction versus repulsion?
cards.back: Netrin’s source and distribution supply the location. The growth cone’s receptors and, in some cells, internal signalling state determine the response’s sign.
cards.quote: Netrin marks a place; the growth cone decides what to do there.
cards.section: The layout

cards.front: Steering of an axon by a diffusing cue is called {{c1::chemotropism}}.
cards.quote: A cue that draws axons toward its source from a distance is a chemoattractant, and steering by a diffusing cue is chemotropism.
cards.section: Something crosses the gel

cards.front: Rat dorsal spinal-cord explants grow few axons alone, but axons grow toward a separate floor-plate explant in collagen. What supports a signal crossing the gel?
cards.back: The tissues never touch, yet the nearby floor plate changes axon growth and direction. Its effect must cross the gap.
cards.quote: The explants were apart, so the effect had to cross the gel.
cards.section: Something crosses the gel

cards.front: Which tissue provided enough material for the original purification of netrin-1 and netrin-2?
cards.back: Membranes from embryonic chick brain.
cards.quote: Membranes from embryonic chick brain had it. Thousands of brains went into the work.
cards.section: From an activity to a molecule

cards.front: During netrin purification, why were fractions from each chromatography step tested on rat spinal-cord explants?
cards.back: Axon outgrowth identified fractions retaining the biological activity, so those fractions could be kept for further purification.
cards.quote: after each step every fraction went back onto rat spinal-cord explants. The axons reported which fractions to keep.
cards.section: From an activity to a molecule

cards.front: Why does increased axon outgrowth in a netrin purification assay fail to establish attraction?
cards.back: Outgrowth measures whether axons grow, not their direction. A cue can promote growth without steering axons toward its source.
cards.quote: The purification assay scored whether axons grew out of an explant, not which way they pointed,
cards.section: From an activity to a molecule

cards.front: How do unc-40 and unc-5 loss distinguish the two responses to ventral UNC-6 in C. elegans?
cards.back: unc-40 loss mainly disrupts movement toward ventral UNC-6; unc-5 loss mainly disrupts movement away. Different readers support opposite directions.
cards.quote: unc-40 mutants have strong defects in movement toward the ventral side and weaker defects in movement away.
cards.section: The worm already knew: one cue, two readers

cards.front: Why does loss of UNC-6 in C. elegans indicate a guidance defect rather than a complete inability to move?
cards.back: Cells and axons still move, but many take the wrong route. The cue helps determine direction rather than simply enabling movement.
cards.quote: Without UNC-6, cells and axons still move, but many take the wrong route.
cards.section: The worm already knew: one cue, two readers

cards.front: C. elegans touch neurons gain UNC-5 and turn dorsally. If UNC-6 is then removed, should the new dorsal route persist, and why?
cards.back: No. The UNC-5-induced dorsal route still requires UNC-6; changing the reader changes the response to the cue, rather than replacing the cue.
cards.quote: With UNC-5, the touch-neuron axons grew dorsally, away from the ventral UNC-6, and this still needed UNC-6.
cards.section: The worm already knew: one cue, two readers

cards.front: Netrin-1 binds cells displaying DCC. What additional functional evidence links DCC to commissural axon outgrowth?
cards.back: An antibody to DCC selectively blocks netrin-evoked outgrowth from spinal explants, linking DCC to the response as well as binding.
cards.quote: An antibody to DCC selectively blocks netrin-evoked outgrowth from spinal explants.
cards.section: The vertebrate readers: DCC and UNC5

cards.front: DCC blockade reduces netrin-evoked outgrowth in culture, and loss of Dcc or netrin-1 gives similar mouse commissural defects. What combined inference is justified?
cards.back: DCC participates in netrin-dependent commissural development in culture and in vivo. The rules are that blocking a reader tests its function and similar cue/reader loss supports a shared pathway; outgrowth alone does not establish steering.
cards.quote: Remove the cue or remove the reader, and commissural axons fail in much the same way.
cards.section: The vertebrate readers: DCC and UNC5

cards.front: Netrin-1 repels trochlear axons in culture, yet these axons are largely normal in netrin-1-mutant mice. How can both observations hold?
cards.back: Culture establishes that netrin can repel these axons; it does not establish that this cue is indispensable in vivo. The lesson’s rule is that other repellents can also guide them.
cards.quote: In the netrin-1 mutant, though, trochlear axons were largely normal, so other repellents also guide them.
cards.section: The vertebrate readers: DCC and UNC5

cards.front: In the fly netrin system, Frazzled is removed while Unc5 remains. Which repulsive response should be lost, and which can remain?
cards.back: Long-range repulsion should be lost; short-range repulsion can remain. Long-range repulsion also requires Frazzled, whereas Unc5 alone suffices at short range.
cards.quote: Unc5 alone is enough for short-range repulsion, and long-range repulsion also needs Frazzled,
cards.section: The vertebrate readers: DCC and UNC5

cards.front: The enzyme PKA is switched on by {{c1::cAMP}}.
cards.quote: protein kinase A (PKA, the enzyme cAMP switches on)
cards.section: Same receptor, opposite turn

cards.front: In the frog spinal growth-cone turning assay, netrin-1 attracts a cone. PKA is then inhibited without removing netrin. What happens and why?
cards.back: The cone turns away. In this frog spinal system, blocking cAMP–PKA signalling changes the sign of the netrin response rather than eliminating it.
cards.quote: The same growth cones turned away. An antibody to DCC stopped both turns, the attraction and the repulsion.
cards.section: Same receptor, opposite turn

cards.front: Why does anti-DCC blocking both attraction and PKA-inhibition-induced repulsion matter in frog spinal growth cones?
cards.back: Both responses require DCC. Internal signalling can reverse the turn without requiring a different receptor in this system.
cards.quote: An antibody to DCC stopped both turns, the attraction and the repulsion.
cards.section: Same receptor, opposite turn

cards.front: An untested axon expresses DCC. Is that enough to predict attraction to netrin, and would the frog result justify predicting repulsion after PKA inhibition?
cards.back: Neither prediction is secure. The rule combines receptor identity with internal state, and the cAMP-dependent reversal was demonstrated in frog spinal growth cones; its direction in another axon requires testing.
cards.quote: This is one worked example in one system, not a rule for every netrin-responsive axon.
cards.section: Same receptor, opposite turn

cards.front: For a steady small source diffusing in three dimensions with no cue loss, what approximates the fractional concentration difference across a narrow growth cone?
cards.back: w/r, where w is growth-cone width and r is distance from the source; concentration follows C = k/r.
cards.quote: fractional difference ≈ w / r (for C = k / r; w = growth cone width, r = distance)
cards.section: In the dish: reading a shallow gradient

cards.front: Use the narrow-cone approximation w/r for C = k/r. A 10 µm growth cone moves from 300 µm to 600 µm from a steady point source with no cue loss. How does its fractional concentration difference change?
cards.back: At 300 µm: 10/300 ≈ 0.0333 = 3.33%. At 600 µm: 10/600 ≈ 0.0167 = 1.67%. Doubling distance halves the approximate fractional difference.
cards.quote: the fractional difference across a growth cone is roughly its width over its distance from the source:
cards.section: In the dish: reading a shallow gradient

cards.front: In the simple receptor-binding model, Kd is the concentration at which {{c1::half}} the receptors are bound.
cards.quote: where Kd is the concentration that fills half the receptors.
cards.section: In the dish: reading a shallow gradient

cards.front: Why does a fixed fractional concentration difference produce little receptor-occupancy contrast far below or far above Kd?
cards.back: Far below Kd, almost no receptors are bound; far above Kd, almost all are. Either extreme leaves little difference between the two sides.
cards.quote: Far below Kd, almost no receptors are bound on either side. Far above it, almost all are.
cards.section: In the dish: reading a shallow gradient

cards.front: In a model growth cone, one side experiences C = Kd and the other C = 2Kd. Using fraction bound = C/(C + Kd), what is the occupancy difference in percentage points?
cards.back: At Kd: 1/(1 + 1) = 0.5 = 50%. At 2Kd: 2/(2 + 1) ≈ 0.6667 = 66.67%. Difference ≈ 16.67 percentage points.
cards.quote: In the simplest binding model the fraction bound is C / (C + Kd),
cards.section: In the dish: reading a shallow gradient

cards.front: How can adaptation restore a growth cone’s response without removing the binding limit at concentrations far from Kd?
cards.back: Resetting the internal baseline prevents a stuck response. If Kd stays unchanged, adaptation still leaves small, noisy occupancy differences far from Kd.
cards.quote: It cannot undo the binding limit: if Kd is unchanged, the occupancy difference is still small and noisy far from Kd.
cards.section: In the dish: reading a shallow gradient

cards.front: How does netrin-1 made by ventricular-zone progenitors reach the path of mouse spinal commissural axons?
cards.back: It travels along progenitor fibres and accumulates at the pial surface along the axons’ route.
cards.quote: The progenitors send their netrin-1 out along their fibres, and it builds up at the pial surface,
cards.section: In the embryo: which source do the axons need?

cards.front: How does haptotaxis differ from chemotropism in axon guidance?
cards.back: Haptotaxis uses a cue bound to a surface; chemotropism uses a diffusing cue.
cards.quote: Guidance by a cue bound to a surface, unlike chemotropism, is called haptotaxis.
cards.section: In the embryo: which source do the axons need?

cards.front: You predict floor-plate netrin supplies the dominant mouse spinal guidance signal. Which result challenges that prediction: most commissural axons staying on course after floor-plate deletion, or many errors after progenitor deletion? Explain the comparison.
cards.back: The combination challenges it: most commissural axons stay on course after removing the proposed dominant source, while removing progenitor netrin causes many axons to go off course. Progenitor-derived netrin therefore supplies much of the guidance in this system.
cards.quote: Without progenitor netrin, many commissural axons went off course.
cards.section: In the embryo: which source do the axons need?

cards.front: Mouse source-specific deletions support a role for progenitor netrin near the pia. Combined with netrin’s ability to diffuse in gel, do they establish surface-contact guidance in vivo?
cards.back: No. The rules are that culture demonstrates a capability and source deletion identifies a needed source. A surface-bound path and a short-range gradient near that path both fit the deletion results.
cards.quote: A deletion shows which source the axons need, not how they read it.
cards.section: In the embryo: which source do the axons need?

cards.front: How did later mouse studies revise the source model suggested by the earlier floor-plate and progenitor netrin deletions?
cards.back: A model in which progenitor-derived netrin does much of the guiding and floor-plate netrin also contributes. A strong requirement for one source does not exclude cooperation with another.
cards.quote: floor plate netrin still contributes, working with progenitor netrin
cards.section: In the embryo: which source do the axons need?

cards.front: Design a culture comparison to distinguish guidance by a diffusing cue from guidance by a surface-bound cue. How should axon growth and direction be scored?
cards.back: Compare a separated secreting source with immobilized cue on a stripe. Score outgrowth separately from turning, including turning from off the stripe. The rules are that turning across a gap supports diffusion, growth confined to bound cue with no turning from a distance supports contact guidance, and outgrowth alone does not establish steering.
cards.quote: Turning at a distance, falling off as the source moves away, supports a diffusible cue.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Axons turn toward a separated cue source and also grow along a stripe of immobilized cue. Must one culture result be wrong, and why?
cards.back: No. The cue can function in both diffusible and bound forms. Passing one assay does not rule out the other mode.
cards.quote: A cue could pass both tests, and netrin can act in both forms in vitro.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: One netrin site is DCC-specific; a second is generic. If UNC5A replaces DCC at the generic site, what response change does the structural model propose?
cards.back: A switch from attraction to repulsion. The proposed mechanism changes receptor occupancy at the generic site; it is a structural proposal, not proof of every axon’s response.
cards.quote: UNC5A can take DCC's place at the generic site, which the authors proposed switches the response from attraction to repulsion
cards.section: Binding sites and a retracted paper

cards.front: In mouse retinal axons, which local guidance step is impaired by loss of netrin-1 or DCC?
cards.back: Local exit through the optic disk, rather than arrival at it. The axons reach the destination but fail at the next local guidance step.
cards.quote: the axons still reach the optic disk but fail to leave through it, so netrin acts locally there.
cards.section: Calcium, laminin and the retinal exit

cards.front: A frog retinal growth cone attracted to netrin encounters laminin-1 at the retinal surface. What change is expected, and why?
cards.back: Netrin can become repulsive. In these frog retinal growth cones, laminin-1 lowers cAMP and converts attraction to repulsion.
cards.quote: laminin-1 turns netrin's attraction into repulsion in frog retinal growth cones, and that laminin-1 lowers their cAMP.
cards.section: Calcium, laminin and the retinal exit

cards.front: Does reversible extracellular-matrix binding alone steepen a netrin concentration profile?
cards.back: No. It holds a bound pool and slows formation of the profile, but does not by itself steepen it.
cards.quote: Reversible binding holds a bound pool and slows how fast the profile forms, but does not by itself steepen it.
cards.section: Real gradients are not ideal

cards.front: In a model of noisy receptor binding, a growth cone averages 16 independent snapshots instead of one. By what factor does noise fall, and does this guarantee reliable detection?
cards.back: Noise falls by about √16 = 4, to approximately one-quarter of its original level. Reliability still depends on whether the signal is large enough relative to the remaining noise.
cards.quote: Averaging M independent snapshots over time cuts the noise by about √M.
cards.section: Real gradients are not ideal

cards.front: For a steady small point source in homogeneous 3D space, compare reversible matrix binding with uniform irreversible removal. When w is much smaller than r and λ, which can keep fractional contrast from falling as low as w/r far away?
cards.back: Irreversible removal: the rule C ∝ e^(−r/λ)/r gives fractional contrast ≈ w(1/r + 1/λ). Reversible binding alone slows profile formation without steepening it. This inference uses the point-source model, not a line or sheet source.
cards.quote: the fractional difference is approximately w(1/r + 1/λ), so far from the source it does not fall as low as w/r.
cards.section: Real gradients are not ideal
